title: Cardiovascular risk associated with first-line Janus kinase inhibitors versus TNF inhibitors in patients with RA: a nationwide cohort study.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) between tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) and Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) when initiated as first-line advanced therapy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). METHODS: Using the Korean nationwide claims database, we identified patients newly diagnosed with RA between 2010 and 2015. Patients who initiated TNFi or JAKi as first-line advanced therapy were selected for analysis. Patients were followed from initiation of TNFi or JAKi through June 2024. The primary outcome was incident MACE, defined as myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or coronary revascularization. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were applied in the total cohort. We additionally performed propensity score (PS)-matched analyses to address confounding by indication. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to baseline cardiovascular risk factors. RESULTS: The study included 6,174 patients (TNFi = 5,152; JAKi = 1,022). The incidence rates of MACE were 4.1 and 3.6 per 1,000 person-years in the TNFi and JAKi groups, respectively. MACE risk did not differ significantly between JAKi and TNFi in the total study cohort (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.636, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.283 to 1.429) or in the PS-matched population (adjusted HR 0.715, 95% CI 0.187 to 2.739). Results were consistent across all prespecified subgroups, including patients with baseline cardiovascular risk factors. CONCLUSION: First-line use of JAKi was not associated with an increased risk of MACE compared with TNFi. These findings provide real-world evidence supporting the cardiovascular safety of JAKi as first-line advanced therapy in patients with RA.

title: Distributional Diagnosis and Calibration with Negative Controls for Outcome-wide Real-world Evidence
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been linked to heterogeneous, potentially pleiotropic effects across organ systems, motivating outcome-wide comparative risk profiling in real-world data. A central challenge in such analyses is residual bias that remains after adjustment for observed confounders, which can distort effect estimates and mis-calibrate uncertainty. We present distributional diagnosis and calibration (DC), which uses panels of negative control outcomes (NCOs) to diagnose residual bias and calibrate uncertainty. DC evaluates null behavior via p -value uniformity and empirical coverage across NCOs, and uses the empirical distribution of NCO effect estimates to calibrate confidence intervals for prespecified primary outcomes. DC is modular: it can wrap around commonly used causal inference methods and operates directly on summary statistics, supporting collaborative research under data-sharing constraints. Using electronic health records from a large U.S. clinical research network (152.7 million patients), we compared GLP-1RAs with sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors across 15 prespecified outcomes spanning cardiovascular, mental health, and genitourinary domains using four causal estimators. Across outcomes and methods, DC diagnostics revealed substantial and method-dependent residual systematic error. DC calibration attenuated systematic error signals observed in negative controls and yielded more stable, better-calibrated estimates for clinical outcomes, supporting DC as a practical strategy to strengthen the credibility of outcome-wide real-world CER. title: Emulating Comparative Oncology Trials With Real-World Evidence Studies (ENCORE): Process Development and Methodological Considerations for Oncology Real-World Data.
abstract: Real-world evidence (RWE) is increasingly used to complement findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), contextualizing the effectiveness and safety of medical interventions as delivered in routine clinical practice. Advances in the curation and accessibility of electronic health record (EHR) data present the opportunity to utilize real-world data (RWD) to investigate therapeutic areas including oncology, where administrative healthcare claims databases alone are often not fit-for-purpose. The RCT DUPLICATE initiative has previously evaluated when RWE can most appropriately draw causal conclusions by emulating trials for nononcology indications. Here, we present the design and trial selection for the emulation of comparative oncology trials with real-world evidence (ENCORE) project, which extends this work to oncology. ENCORE is designed to emulate 12 RCTs in four oncology-specialized EHR databases across four different cancer indications, specifically non-small-cell lung cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and multiple myeloma. It will place special emphasis on systematic evaluation of fitness of data in relation to the study design and statistical analysis for a particular research question and preregistration of study protocols prior to initiation and analysis. Prespecified criteria will assess agreement of treatment effect estimates between RCTs and their respective emulations. Through extensive sensitivity analyses benchmarked against RCT results, the ENCORE project aims to inform understanding of how measurement, design, and analytic decisions influence the interpretation of results from emulated oncology trials using RWD.

title: Real world evidence for glucosamine-chondroitin-calcium supplementation on joint pain.
abstract: Background Joint and bone diseases are major causes of morbidity worldwide. While glucosamine sulfate (GS) and chondroitin sulfate (CS) have demonstrated benefits in severe degenerative joint conditions, real-world evidence on the use patterns and reported outcomes of their combination with calcium (GCC) among individuals with mild-to-moderate joint discomfort remains limited. Methods This real-world study enrolled 9,090 adults who used GCC for ≥1 month and completed an online questionnaire; pre- and post-use symptom scores were analyzed among participants reporting joint symptoms or back pain. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for demographics, lifestyle, comorbidities, medications, and other dietary supplement use. Results After GCC use, joint pain, stiffness, swelling, inflexibility and back pain scores were significantly lower than pre-use scores, with mean changes of -1.74 (95% CI: -1.81 to -1.68) for joint pain and -1.37 (95% CI: -1.45 to -1.28) for back pain (all P Conclusion Although the mean changes did not reach the pre-specified primary two-point minimal clinically important difference, GCC use was associated with lower joint discomfort and back pain scores, and self-reported adverse events were rare.

title: Real-world evidence and observational studies: Methodological challenges in clinical research.
abstract: The emergence of real-world evidence (RWE) has significantly broadened the scope of clinical research in internal medicine, providing insights that extend beyond the constraints of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). RWE is generated from real-world data (RWD)-information collected outside experimental settings, such as routine clinical practice. Observational studies, including cohort, case-control and cross-sectional designs, are fundamental to RWE generation, enabling the examination of patient outcomes, treatment patterns and disease epidemiology as they naturally occur. The expanded use of registries and electronic health records (EHRs) has revolutionized data collection, offering both depth and breadth for large-scale, longitudinal studies. However, drawing causal inferences from observational research presents substantial methodological challenges, as confounding and bias arising from non-randomized treatment allocation and unmeasured variables can distort results. Data quality issues-such as missing data, exposure and outcome misclassification, and inconsistent variable definitions-further complicate analysis. Advanced statistical techniques, including propensity score matching and instrumental variable analysis, have been developed to mitigate the limitations due to confounding, yet cannot fully substitute for randomization. Transparent reporting, pre-registration of protocols, and adherence to standardized guidelines (e.g. STROBE) are essential to enhance rigor and reproducibility. Despite their challenges, observational studies remain indispensable for addressing clinical questions that cannot be answered by RCTs, informing practice and guiding healthcare policy. Careful study design, rigorous analysis and transparent reporting are crucial for maximizing the reliability and impact of real-world evidence in internal medicine.

title: Objective study validity diagnostics: a framework requiring pre-specified, empirical verification to increase trust in the reliability of real-world evidence.
abstract: Objective Propose a framework to empirically evaluate and report validity of findings from observational studies using pre-specified objective diagnostics, increasing trust in real-world evidence (RWE). Materials and methods The framework employs objective diagnostic measures to assess the appropriateness of study designs, analytic assumptions, and threats to validity in generating reliable evidence addressing causal questions. Diagnostic evaluations should be interpreted before the unblinding of study results or, alternatively, only unblind results from analyses that pass pre-specified thresholds. We provide a conceptual overview of objective diagnostic measures and demonstrate their impact on the validity of RWE from a large-scale comparative new-user study of various antihypertensive medications. We evaluated expected absolute systematic error (EASE) before and after applying diagnostic thresholds, using a large set of negative control outcomes. Results Applying objective diagnostics reduces bias and improves evidence reliability in observational studies. Among 11 716 analyses (EASE = 0.38), 13.9% met pre-specified diagnostic thresholds which reduced EASE to zero. Objective diagnostics provide a comprehensive and empirical set of tests that increase confidence when passed and raise doubts when failed. Discussion The increasing use of real-world data presents a scientific opportunity; however, the complexity of the evidence generation process poses challenges for understanding study validity and trusting RWE. Deploying objective diagnostics is crucial to reducing bias and improving reliability in RWE generation. Under ideal conditions, multiple study designs pass diagnostics and generate consistent results, deepening understanding of causal relationships. Open-source, standardized programs can facilitate implementation of diagnostic analyses. Conclusion Objective diagnostics are a valuable addition to the RWE generation process.
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA

title: Preregistration: A Key to Credible Real-World Evidence Generation.
abstract: Background Preregistration of study protocols in a public repository promotes transparency and reproducibility in pharmacoepidemiological research. Despite its clear benefits, preregistration remains underutilized. Purpose Here, we discuss the advantages of preregistration, explore barriers to its implementation, and highlight existing repositories for preregistering real-world evidence study protocols. A relatively new option is the Real-World Evidence Registry within the Open Science Framework (OSF), which we briefly introduce.

title: A Bias-Aware Analytic Framework for Real-World Data with AI-Audited Workflows: Application to Opioid Ordering in Pediatric Oncology
abstract: Background: The growing use of computational modeling of real-world data (RWD) in clinical research introduces significant risks for data scientists already managing inconsistency, unexamined bias, and analytical opacity. Without the formal theory supporting biostatistical models and despite more than 600 guideline-based checklists for data quality and transparency reporting in observational RWD, reliance on ad hoc model specification and verification is still the norm. No structured guidance exists to help clinicians and researchers systematically assess and manage the risks generated by computational results using RWD. In this paper, we propose a framework that reflects a rigorous, bias-aware methodology for complex analyses of RWD. We also propose the curated use of a large language model (LLM) supporting AI-generated code-auditing to ensure data quality. Our structured hierarchical approach coupled with AI-auditing is the first phase in the development of full-stack automation of RWD analytic validation. Methods Our analytic framework spans 10 domains across three analytic phases. Each domain includes prespecified criteria governing verification with potential biases, mechanisms, and mitigation strategies systematically mapped throughout. Phase 1 entails Specification (Domains 1–4: objectives and estimands, data inputs and outputs, cohort and filters, and variable coding); Phase 2:Modeling (Domains 5–7: model testing, diagnostics, and reasonableness checks); and Phase 3: Robustness and Interpretation (Domains 8–10: missing data handling, temporal and stratified checks, and scope boundaries). We utilize specific prompt-directed large language model (LLM) auditing of model elements to ensure data quality. The methodology is illustrated with examples from an empirical characterization of inpatient opioid data from Cerner Real World (2014–2021). Results The Cerner RWD data base contained 16,734 pediatric cancer patients (76,395 encounters) across 55 U.S. health systems. During the specification phase, total daily dose could not be estimated with sufficient validity from Cerner RWD, and “as-needed” orders, warranted empirically supported exclusion. The modeling phase revealed residual variability in opioid ordering attributable primarily to patient-level differences within health systems (ICC=19.9%) rather than between health systems (ICC=2.0%). Temporal analysis revealed a downward trend in morphine and fentanyl ordering trajectories from 2017-onward. We then utilized curated prompting to enforce an AI-generated coding requirement to produce valid likelihood ratio tests across the prespecified model sequence accounting for temporal trends. Conclusions The 10-domain framework provides a structured, reproducible mechanism for governing RWD analyses, supporting transparent exposure definition, systematic bias assessment, prespecified analytic decision-making, and auditing via curated AI prompting. To our knowledge, this is the first structured framework to 1) identify analytic metrics at risk for unreliability; 2) incorporate AI-audited workflows in RWD research; and 3) demonstrate utility in a large multi-institutional real-world data base. The approach reflects the initial development in automating of RWE data analytics.

title: A mortality model for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma: emulation of subjective life expectancy criteria from a clinical trial in real-world data.
abstract: Patients with limited life expectancy (LE) are often excluded from oncology trials based on subjective judgment, posing a challenge when contextualizing trial findings with real-world data (RWD). This study evaluated the feasibility of modeling mortality in RWD for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) to replicate patient exclusion (LE < 6 months) for application in an external control arm study.A targeted literature review (TLR, January 2016-March 2022) was performed to identify mortality prediction models in RRMM. Because no suitable model was found, a de novo mortality model was developed using the COTA database.Twenty-one prognostic factors identified via literature review and clinical experts were included in the models. Cox proportional hazards models with bootstrap validation to correct for optimism were used to identify the best-performing model. A threshold of ≥50% predicted mortality probability within 6 months of the start of the line of therapy (LOT) was used for sensitivity and specificity estimates.Patients (N = 1,112) contributed 2,626 LOTs. A model with the top 20 prognostic factors maximized concordance and accuracy while achieving pre-specified performance thresholds, except for the F1 score. The predicted and observed 6-month mortality probability were both 26%.Mortality prediction for RRMM remains challenging with RWD. The de novo model exhibited strong discrimination performance but low F1 score, suggesting it may be useful to identify patients at highest risk who may be least likely to meet trial LE criteria.

title: Advancing real-world evidence harmonization: lessons from the UK, EMA and global policy frameworks.
abstract: Aim: Real-world evidence (RWE) - defined here as clinical evidence derived from the analysis of real-world data (RWD) on patient health status and healthcare delivery - has become a cornerstone of regulatory and health technology assessment (HTA) decision making. However, despite broad consensus on its value, policy frameworks governing RWE generation and evaluation remain heterogeneous across jurisdictions. Importantly, this heterogeneity partly reflects the distinct purposes for which RWE is used, including regulatory safety assessment, effectiveness evaluation, health-economic modeling and natural-history research. These functional differences are not inherently problematic; however, fragmented operational requirements can create duplication, inefficiency and delays in patient access. Materials & methods: This study employed a narrative comparative policy review of RWE guidance issued by twelve major regulatory and HTA agencies, including the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), the EMA, the US FDA and the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH). Frameworks were compared across four domains: data quality, statistical methods, registry governance and transparency. Harmonization is defined as alignment across these domains sufficient to enable consistent planning, analysis and interpretation of RWE across jurisdictions, rather than uniformity of decision making. Results: The analysis identified convergence in high-level principles but persistent divergence in operational expectations. The MHRA emphasizes flexibility and scientific dialogue; the EMA prioritizes consistency and structured governance; and the FDA provides comprehensive but resource-intensive guidance, reflecting detailed documentation requirements, prespecified analytic expectations and extensive methodological review. HTA bodies apply additional evidentiary criteria related to comparative effectiveness and value, sustaining functional fragmentation even within the same healthcare systems. Conclusion: RWE fragmentation reflects both legitimate functional differences and avoidable operational misalignment. Progress toward harmonization therefore requires shared minimum standards and transparency mechanisms rather than additional guidance documents. The UK's post-Brexit autonomy positions it as a test environment for collaborative pilots with the European Medicines Agency, the International Council for Harmonization (ICH) and the International Coalition of Medicines Regulatory Authorities (ICMRA). Six strategic actions are proposed to support pragmatic alignment while preserving contextual flexibility.

title: Anterior Lumbar Interbody Fusion Versus Total Disc Replacement with a Viscoelastic Prosthesis for Single-Level Lumbar Degenerative Disc Disease in Young Adults: A Comparative Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The optimal surgical approach for patients with lumbar degenerative disc disease (DDD) remains a subject of ongoing debate, particularly when comparing anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) and total disc replacement (TDR). The primary objective of this study was to compare short-term outcomes between these two surgical approaches in terms of clinical efficacy, patient satisfaction, and safety profile. The secondary objective was to evaluate patient-specific variables associated with postoperative improvement in order to identify potential factors that may guide a personalized surgical strategy. Methods: This retrospective, single-center observational study included 87 patients who underwent single-level lumbar surgery using either an ALIF (n = 38) or TDR (n = 49) approach between January 2021 and May 2025. Eligible patients were younger than 45 years and had complete preoperative, intraoperative, and 1-year follow-up data. Demographic, clinical, preoperative, and intraoperative variables, as well as patient satisfaction and quality-of-life improvement, were collected, analyzed, and compared between groups. The primary between-group analysis used analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with adjustment for baseline outcome values and prespecified confounders (age, sex, body mass index, smoking status, ASA class). Longitudinal effects were assessed using a linear model with treatment × time interaction and cluster-robust standard errors. A formal smoking × surgical-strategy interaction was tested in a multivariable regression on 12-month Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) change. Reporting followed the STROBE guidelines for observational studies. Results: Both groups showed substantial within-group improvement at all follow-up time points (all p < 0.05 except ALIF leg pain at 6 months; paired Wilcoxon test). Baseline-adjusted between-group comparisons (ANCOVA) showed a numerically modest early difference favoring TDR for Visual Analogue Score (VAS) low-back pain at 3 and 6 months (adjusted Δ = -1.46, 95% CI -2.63 to -0.30, p = 0.016 at 3 months; -1.35, 95% CI -2.63 to -0.07, p = 0.043 at 6 months), below the minimum clinically important difference of 2 points though neither survived Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. The formal treatment × time interaction test was not significant for any outcome (ODI p = 0.39; VAS back p = 0.29; VAS leg p = 0.06. Overall, 92% of patients in the ALIF group and 86% of patients in the TDR group reported being satisfied or very satisfied, and 60-72% of patients returned to work. Radiographic analysis in the TDR group showed maintained segmental mobility, with median range of motion of 4.0° (IQR 2.0-8.0°) overall (median 6.0°, IQR 4.0-8.5° at L4-L5; 3.0°, IQR 2.0-6.0° at L5-S1). A multivariable regression model on 12-month ODI change, adjusted for age, sex, BMI, ASA class, and baseline ODI, showed a highly significant smoking-burden × surgical-strategy interaction (dose-response smoker code × TDR coefficient = -9.47, 95% CI -15.6 to -3.3, p = 0.004): higher preoperative smoking burden was associated with reduced ODI improvement specifically in the TDR group (Spearman r = -0.41, p = 0.004) but not the ALIF group (Spearman r = +0.17, p = 0.32). Conclusions: This cohort study suggests that both ALIF and TDR were associated with substantial clinical improvement and high patient satisfaction at 1 year postoperatively; because treatment selection was not randomized, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of comparative effectiveness. A modest early difference favoring TDR was observed for VAS low-back pain (below the minimum clinically important difference); no statistically significant between-group differences were demonstrated for any outcome after correction for multiple comparisons. The observed associations between 1-year ODI improvement and patient-specific variables require confirmation in larger independent cohorts. The finding of a significant smoking-burden × surgical-strategy interaction is an exploratory and hypothesis-generating and, if confirmed in prospective cohorts, may inform preoperative optimization strategies for TDR candidates.

title: Beyond Parametric and Nonparametric Tests: A Practical Guide to Table 1 in Clinical Research.
abstract: In many clinical research reports, Table 1 presents the baseline or general characteristics of study participants and helps readers understand the study population and observed between-group differences. Despite its apparent simplicity, constructing and interpreting Table 1 requires several distinct decisions, including whether formal between-group inference is scientifically justified, how variables should be summarized, and how observed differences should be interpreted. Routine significance testing of baseline characteristics is generally discouraged in randomized trials and often provides limited information in observational studies, where group differences may reflect treatment selection, exposure patterns, disease severity, or other systematic mechanisms. We propose a purpose-first framework in which investigators first clarify the intended role of Table 1, consider the study design, and determine whether a comparison addresses a prespecified and scientifically meaningful inferential question. They should then identify the variable type, evaluate distributional shape, influential observations, and clinical interpretability, and select appropriate summary statistics. For descriptive applications, transparent group-specific summaries should be emphasized, with observed absolute or standardized differences added when useful and without routine p-values. Confidence intervals should be reported when a population-level estimation objective has been defined. When formal inference is justified, investigators should define the target quantity or estimand and select a statistical method according to the variable type, data structure, distributional characteristics, and model assumptions. Effect estimates and confidence intervals should receive greater emphasis than isolated p-values. This framework distinguishes description from inference and promotes transparent, statistically coherent, and clinically meaningful construction and interpretation of Table 1.

title: Biomaterials in Retinal Surgery: Engineering the Future.
abstract: Purpose To review current and emerging biomaterials in retinal surgery-vitreous tamponade agents, retinal prostheses, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplant scaffolds, intraocular drug delivery platforms, and gene therapy vectors-with emphasis on the authors' oxime-crosslinked hyaluronic acid vitreous substitute. Design Narrative expert review. Systematic review methodology was not used; no protocol registration, prespecified eligibility criteria, dual independent screening, or PRISMA flow diagram was undertaken. Subjects, participants, and/or controls Published preclinical animal studies, Phase I to III clinical trials, US Food and Drug Administration approvals, and real-world evidence on biomaterials in posterior segment surgery. No individual patient data were accessed. Methods, intervention, or testing A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, supplemented by Google Scholar, was performed from January 2018 to March 2026 across 5 domains: vitreous tamponade agents; retinal prostheses; scaffold-based RPE transplantation; nanoparticle and sustained-release drug delivery; and gene therapy vectors. Peer-reviewed investigations, trial reports, and regulatory data were prioritized. The authors' preclinical hydrogel data are presented as original data within a review context. Main outcome measures Best-corrected visual acuity, intraocular pressure, electroretinography, retinal microstructure on optical coherence tomography, prosthetic visual acuity, ellipsoid zone area loss, injection frequency, and in vivo biocompatibility. Results The PRIMA photovoltaic subretinal implant produced a clinically meaningful improvement in visual acuity in 26 of 32 patients (81%) with geographic atrophy at 12 months. A 44-channel suprachoroidal prosthesis showed no device-related serious adverse events at 2.7 years. The authors' oxime-crosslinked hyaluronic acid hydrogel demonstrated density 1.01 g/mL and refractive index 1.356, with preserved electroretinography and intraocular pressure of 13.5 to 25.9 mmHg in rabbits. Scaffold-based RPE transplantation has entered Phase I/IIa trials. 2025 approvals included a refillable ranibizumab port delivery system for diabetic retinopathy and the first encapsulated cell therapy implant for macular telangiectasia type 2. Three Phase 3 anti-VEGF gene therapy trials are ongoing. Conclusions Biomaterial engineering is transforming retinal disease management from stabilization toward tissue replacement and vision restoration. Principal limitations are the preclinical status of the hydrogel data and early-phase status of RPE scaffold trials. Outstanding challenges include long-term in vivo stability, immunological management of allogeneic constructs, scalable manufacturing, and definitive efficacy trials.

title: C-reactive protein-albumin-lymphocyte index and coronary microvascular dysfunction after primary percutaneous coronary intervention: The mediating role of insulin resistance.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The C-reactive protein-albumin-lymphocyte (CALLY) index integrates systemic inflammation, nutritional status, and immune function. We investigated its association with angiography-derived microvascular resistance (AMR)-defined coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and performed an exploratory statistical mediation analysis involving estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR). METHODS: This retrospective, single-center observational study included 456 consecutive patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI. AMR-defined CMD was prespecified as AMR ≥250 mmHg·s/m. Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS), and prespecified subgroup analyses were performed. Sensitivity and exploratory mediation analyses were also performed. RESULTS: AMR-defined CMD was present in 228 patients (50.0%). In Model 3, each doubling of CALLY was associated with lower odds of AMR-defined CMD (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.80-0.94; P < 0.001). Compared with Q1, Q3 and Q4 were associated with 44% (OR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.32-0.97; P = 0.037) and 52% (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.28-0.84; P = 0.010) lower odds, respectively (P for trend = 0.018). RCS analysis showed an overall association (P = 0.001) without evidence of nonlinearity (P = 0.310). No significant subgroup interactions were observed. Exploratory mediation analysis estimated that eGDR statistically accounted for 15.47% of the observed association. CONCLUSIONS: Higher CALLY values were inversely associated with AMR-defined CMD after primary PCI for STEMI. eGDR may account for part of this association. CALLY may serve as an auxiliary marker for AMR-defined CMD risk stratification, pending prospective multicenter validation.

title: Cardiovascular and mortality outcomes with JAK versus TNF inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis: a target trial emulation (CARDINAL-RA).
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aims to compare cardiovascular and mortality outcomes of Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) versus tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) at elevated cardiovascular risk using target trial emulation. METHODS: Within TriNetX, adults with RA aged ≥50 years and ≥1 cardiovascular risk factor initiating JAKi or TNFi were compared in a new-user, active-comparator design. Improved 1:1 propensity score matching incorporated demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, comorbidities, individual conventional synthetic DMARDs, oral corticosteroids, prior non-TNF biologic exposure, and baseline inflammatory markers. The primary outcome was MACE (nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal ischemic stroke); the secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, and venous thromboembolism (VTE), with cataract as a prespecified negative control. Follow-up began 90 days after initiation. Cox models estimated hazard ratios, with 5-year Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidences and absolute risk differences per 1,000. Cohorts were separately matched by agent, sex, cardiovascular-risk stratum, and index era; E-values quantified sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. RESULTS: In 18,757 matched pairs, JAKi was not associated with excess MACE (HR 1.002, 0.923-1.088; +2.11 per 1,000). All-cause mortality, a secondary outcome, was higher with JAKi (HR 1.158, 1.058-1.268; p = 0.0014; +10.4 per 1,000; E-value 1.586), whereas heart failure hospitalization (HR 1.019, 0.955-1.088) and VTE (HR 1.054, 0.961-1.156) did not differ; the negative control showed no excess (HR 0.934, 0.867-1.007). No agent showed a significant excess in MACE or mortality (mortality HR 1.052 tofacitinib, 1.213 baricitinib, and 1.090 upadacitinib); the only nominally significant agent-level finding was VTE with baricitinib (HR 1.364, 1.028-1.809; 198 events). A three-component composite including death was non-significant (HR 1.058, 0.992-1.127). No consistent effect modification was seen by sex, cardiovascular risk burden, or index year. CONCLUSION: JAKi initiation was not associated with excess MACE (primary outcome), heart failure hospitalization, or VTE. A modest excess in all-cause mortality was observed as a secondary outcome, with no signal for any individual agent. This association was of modest robustness (E-value 1.586) and was not reproduced in any agent-specific cohort, so residual channeling bias cannot be excluded. The null MACE result should not be read as class-wide cardiovascular safety reassurance nor the mortality signal as an established causal effect.

title: Cardiovascular events in aging Japanese people with hemophilia: a 3-year interim analysis of the ADVANCE Japan cohort.
abstract: As life expectancy increases in people with hemophilia (PWH), cardiovascular disease (CVD) has emerged as an important comorbidity. However, prospective data on CVD occurrence and its clinical management remain limited. We performed a prespecified 3-year interim analysis of ADVANCE Japan, an ongoing 10-year multicenter prospective cohort study of PWH aged ≥ 40 years, to describe CVD occurrence, clinical management, bleeding outcomes, and associated changes in hemostatic treatment. We also explored factors associated with CVD occurrence using Cox proportional hazards models. Among 588 participants, 24 developed CVD, yielding 26 events over 3 years (cumulative incidence, 4.1%). Ischemic heart disease was the most frequent event. Exploratory analyses suggested that older age, dyslipidemia, and current smoking were associated with CVD occurrence, although estimates were imprecise because of the limited number of events. Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy was administered to selected patients, and hemostatic management was frequently modified following CVD events. One major bleeding event was observed among patients receiving antithrombotic therapy. This prespecified interim analysis provides prospective real-world data on the occurrence and clinical management of CVD in aging Japanese PWH. Risk factor analyses should be considered exploratory, and continued follow-up is required to define long-term cardiovascular risk and outcomes in this population.

title: Changing global prevalence of diuretic resistance amongst patients with heart failure: a systematic review and cumulative meta-analyses.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diuretic resistance (DR) is a major challenge in the management of heart failure, contributing to persistent congestion, prolonged hospitalization, and adverse outcomes. However, inconsistent DR definitions and study designs have resulted in uncertain prevalence estimates and limited guideline development. OBJECTIVE: To determine the pooled prevalence of DR in heart failure using studies with valid heart-failure denominators and extractable binary DR events, and to evaluate the stability and heterogeneity of prevalence estimates over time. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Science Citation Index, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects were searched from 2000 through the final updated search in 2026, supplemented by reference screening. STUDY SELECTION: Observational studies and randomized studies relevant to DR in adults with heart failure were considered for the systematic review. For the quantitative prevalence analysis, studies were required to include an unselected or consecutively assembled heart-failure denominator and an extractable binary DR event count based on a prespecified or study-defined criterion arising after cohort entry. Studies enrolling only patients with established DR, reporting only continuous diuretic-response measures, or lacking a valid binary DR numerator were excluded from prevalence pooling but could remain relevant to the qualitative systematic review. Two reviewers independently extracted data. Prevalence was pooled on the logit scale using an inverse-variance random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation of between-study variance and Hartung-Knapp inference. Heterogeneity, prediction intervals, cumulative meta-analysis, influence and sensitivity analyses, a generalized linear mixed-model robustness analysis, and exploratory funnel-plot asymmetry testing were undertaken. RESULTS: Twelve prevalence-eligible studies involving 24,904 patients were included in the quantitative prevalence analysis, of whom 4,861 met study-defined criteria for DR. The pooled prevalence was 23.0% (95% CI, 13.6%-36.2%), with substantial heterogeneity (I²=98.5%; τ²=0.851; Q=757.17, df=11; p<0.001). The 95% prediction interval was 3.4%-71.6%. A generalized linear mixed model yielded a similar pooled prevalence of 22.5% (95% CI, 14.5%-33.2%). Cumulative analysis showed that the estimate changed as new eligible studies accrued, reaching 23.0% after inclusion of the most recent studies. Exploratory regression analysis did not demonstrate statistically significant funnel-plot asymmetry (p=0.072). CONCLUSION: Approximately one in four patients with heart failure meets a study-defined criterion for DR in prevalence-eligible cohorts. However, the very wide prediction interval and extreme heterogeneity show that DR frequency is strongly dependent on population, setting, timing of assessment, and operational definition. Standardized diagnostic criteria and prospectively assembled prevalence cohorts are required to improve comparability and guide clinical practice.

title: Clinical outcomes and prognostic factors after first- and second-line immunotherapy in a cohort of 57 patients with refractory autoimmune encephalitis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Refractory autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is a severe condition with limited real-world evidence on treatment outcomes and prognostic factors. This study evaluated clinical outcomes and factors associated with 6-month functional recovery in a strictly defined refractory AE cohort. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study screened 246 potentially eligible AE records from 2018 to 2025 and included 57 patients who fulfilled the prespecified refractory AE criteria and had ascertainable 6-month functional outcomes. Second-line immunotherapy was subsequently administered to a subset of patients. The primary outcome was 6-month functional status assessed by the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) after refractory-state adjudication, with favorable outcome defined as mRS 0-2. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for baseline severity and constrained by the limited number of unfavorable outcomes, examined factors associated with 6-month functional outcome. RESULTS: All 57 patients fulfilled the harmonized refractory criterion after inadequate response to first-line immunotherapy. Second-line escalation was subsequently administered to 14 patients (24.6%), whereas 43 (75.4%) did not receive second-line therapy. Favorable 6-month outcomes occurred in 9/14 (64.3%) and 28/43 (65.1%), respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In the parsimonious multivariable analysis, higher mRS at refractory-state adjudication and ICU admission were associated with unfavorable 6-month functional outcome. The association with ICU admission persisted after adjustment for mRS, but its magnitude was imprecisely estimated and likely overlaps with the underlying construct of disease severity. These findings should therefore be considered exploratory prognostic associations rather than definitive independent predictors.

title: Clinical outcomes of tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis using a retrograde femoral nail versus a dedicated hindfoot fusion nail in charcot neuroarthropathy: A prospective observational study in a resource-limited setting.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Dedicated hindfoot fusion nail (HFN) systems for Charcot tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis may be unavailable or unaffordable in resource-limited settings. A retrograde femoral nail (RFN) can serve as a pragmatic contingency implant when a dedicated HFN is unavailable. This study compared functional, radiographic, union, complication, and implant acquisition-cost outcomes between RFN and HFN. METHODS: A prospective, non-randomized, two-arm observational study was conducted in 60 patients undergoing TTC arthrodesis for Charcot neuroarthropathy, consecutively allocated to RFN (n = 30) or HFN (n = 30) according to implant availability. Patients were followed for 24 months. Functional outcomes (AOFAS, VAS, ODI, FAAM), radiographic union, complications, and implant acquisition costs were assessed. Multivariable linear regression adjusted the 24-month AOFAS comparison for prespecified baseline covariates. RESULTS: At 24 months, no statistically significant between-group differences were detected in functional outcomes (AOFAS: 77.76 vs. 78.24, p = 0.800). RFN had a lower implant acquisition cost (USD 2126 vs. USD 3374; mean difference -USD 1248, p < 0.001), although this represents implant cost only and not total treatment cost. Radiographic union occurred in 27/30 RFN patients (90%) and 30/30 HFN patients (100%) (absolute risk difference -10%, 95% CI -26% to +3%; p = 0.237). Among patients who achieved radiographic union, the observed time to union was 12.8 versus 14.4 weeks; however, this difference is of uncertain clinical relevance and excludes the three RFN nonunions. CONCLUSION: In this prospective observational cohort, RFN was associated with broadly similar measured functional outcomes and complication rates to HFN when the dedicated implant was unavailable. The study does not establish equivalence or biomechanical interchangeability. The three RFN nonunions are clinically more important than the small difference in time to radiographic union. RFN may therefore be considered a pragmatic contingency option in resource-limited settings, while purpose-designed HFN remains the preferred dedicated implant when available.

title: Clinical, Functional, and Radiological Profile of Patients With Spondyloarthritis: A Cross-Sectional Study From a Tertiary Care Center in Central India.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) includes a group of chronic inflammatory rheumatic disorders, such as ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, enteropathic arthritis, and undifferentiated SpA, unified by shared genetic, clinical, and immunopathological features. Comprehensive clinical profiling of SpA patients, including disease activity, functional status, and structural complications such as vertebral fracture, remains limited in Indian tertiary care settings. This study aims to describe the sociodemographic, clinical, radiological, and biochemical profile of patients with SpA, including disease activity and functional status using validated indices (Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score with C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP), and Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Functional Index (BASFI)), and to assess associations between these measures, inflammatory markers, and the presence of vertebral fractures, a structural complication anticipated to be uncommon in this cohort. METHODS: This hospital-based, cross-sectional, observational study was conducted in the Department of General Medicine of a tertiary care teaching hospital. Fifty adult patients diagnosed with SpA per the European Spondyloarthropathy Study Group (ESSG) criteria were enrolled by consecutive sampling. We performed detailed clinical evaluation, radiological assessment (modified New York criteria for sacroiliitis and vertebral fracture), and laboratory investigations (including HLA-B27 typing). Disease activity and function were assessed using BASDAI, ASDAS-CRP, and BASFI. Data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA); categorical variables were compared using the chi-square/Fisher's exact test and continuous variables using the Student's t-test/Mann-Whitney U test, with p<0.05 considered statistically significant. Given the anticipated small number of vertebral fracture events, all fracture-related comparisons were pre-specified as exploratory. RESULTS: The cohort had a mean age of 41.8 ± 10.9 years with a male predominance (74%). Ankylosing spondylitis was the most common subtype (54%), and axial involvement was present in 56% of patients; HLA-B27 was positive in 80%. Musculoskeletal (enthesitis, dactylitis) and extra-articular manifestations were noted in 64% of patients overall, most commonly enthesitis (38%) and uveitis (16%). Radiologically, 54% had grade III-IV sacroiliitis, and 12% (n=6) had vertebral fractures (predominantly thoracic, 50%). Fracture prevalence was numerically higher with longer disease duration (p=0.018) and higher erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)/C-reactiive protein (CRP) (p=0.038 and p=0.021, respectively). High disease activity was observed in 72% of patients (BASDAI ≥4.0) and 74% (ASDAS-CRP >2.1); 68% had moderate-to-severe functional limitation (BASFI ≥4.0). CONCLUSION: Spondyloarthritis in this cohort predominantly affected young to middle-aged men from rural and lower socioeconomic backgrounds, with a high burden of active disease and structural damage. Vertebral fractures were more frequent with longer disease duration and higher inflammatory markers in this exploratory analysis. The need for early diagnosis, routine disease-activity monitoring, and clinical vigilance for vertebral fracture as an under-recognized structural complication is imperative in resource-limited settings.

title: Comparative cost analysis of Eluvia™ versus Zilver® PTX® in treating femoropopliteal peripheral artery disease utilizing real-world data.
abstract: Aim: To compare the hospital-based costs among patients with femoropopliteal artery (FPA) disease treated with Eluvia™ versus Zilver® PTX® drug-eluting stents using a large real-world USA hospital database. Materials & methods: This retrospective study included adults in the Premier Healthcare Database who underwent lower extremity FPA endovascular revascularization with Eluvia or Zilver PTX between 1 April 2019 and 31 March 2022. Total hospital-based costs during the index procedure and cumulative 1- and 2-year post-discharge follow-up were compared using multivariable generalized linear models adjusted for age, sex, race and baseline chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) status. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted by care setting (hospital inpatient and hospital outpatient) and among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and CLTI. Results: A total of 7208 patients were included, comprising 4218 treated with Eluvia and 2990 treated with Zilver PTX. Patients treated with Eluvia had a higher prevalence of several comorbidities, including congestive heart failure and CKD. Unadjusted mean hospital-based index procedure costs were similar between groups (Eluvia, $28,631 vs Zilver PTX, $28,359; difference, -$272; p = 0.7233). After adjustment, mean index procedure hospital-based costs did not differ significantly between treatment groups ($30,031, p = 0.8491). However, Eluvia was associated with lower adjusted cumulative hospital-based costs at the 1-year (difference, $4,017; p = 0.0066) and 2-year (difference, $6250; p = 0.0021) follow-up. Similar associations were observed in the hospital inpatient and CKD subgroups, whereas no statistically significant differences were observed in the CLTI subgroup. Conclusion: Across patients undergoing femoropopliteal endovascular revascularization, Eluvia was associated with significantly lower post-discharge cumulative hospital-based follow-up costs than Zilver PTX while index procedure costs were comparable. These findings reflect hospital-based costs captured within participating hospitals and do not include medication costs or costs of care received outside the Premier Healthcare Database; therefore, they should not be interpreted as total healthcare costs.

title: Comparative Outcomes of Beta-Blockers vs Non-Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Determining the most effective medication regimen to manage blood pressure and heart rate in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) continues to lack a clear clinical consensus. Although beta-blockers (BBs) are widely prescribed, their negative chronotropic effects may worsen exercise intolerance. Alternative agents like verapamil and diltiazem, which belong to the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (non-DHP CCB) class, offer a physiological alternative, yet comparative data are scarce. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted, comparing BBs vs non-DHP CCBs in adults with HFpEF (left ventricular ejection fraction ≥ 50%). A literature search across key databases was conducted up until May 2026. Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality and heart failure (HF) hospitalization. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were calculated using a random-effects analytical framework incorporating the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman variance correction. Evidence certainty was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Of the 576 retrieved records, two observational cohorts (106,848 patients) met the inclusion criteria. Only one of the two eligible cohorts analyzed real patient-level data; the other was generated. The two-study pooled estimates are reported as exploratory: all-cause mortality HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.34-2.26; p = 0.336) and HF hospitalization HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.34-2.42; p = 0.446), with I² > 80% for both outcomes. At k = 2, these dispersion statistics are themselves unstable, and the pooled intervals are not clinically interpretable. Restricted to the single real-world cohort, the estimates were HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.80-0.85) and HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.91-1.05), respectively, which are the figures of one observational study and carry no meta-analytic weight. Cardiovascular mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, exercise capacity, and quality of life were prespecified but reported by neither study in poolable form. The confidence in these findings was rated as very low because the data stem from observational research and exhibit significant statistical variability alongside wide CIs. Current evidence does not demonstrate the prognostic superiority of either BBs or non-DHP CCBs in HFpEF. Given the very low certainty of the available data and high clinical heterogeneity, pharmacological selection should remain individualized. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to inform clinical guidelines.

title: Contemporary outcomes after 100 consecutive HeartMate 3 LVAD implantations: a single-centre cohort study from a Swiss tertiary centre.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The HeartMate 3 left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is an established therapy for advanced heart failure, yet contemporary real-world data from low- or medium-volume centres remain limited. We aimed to describe the characteristics, management and clinical outcomes of patients undergoing HeartMate 3 LVAD implantation at a Swiss tertiary centre. METHODS: We conducted an observational study including consecutive adult patients who underwent HeartMate 3 implantation at Lausanne University Hospital between November 2015 and January 2026. Baseline characteristics, INTERMACS profiles, perioperative data, survival and LVAD-related complications were assessed. The primary outcome was survival on LVAD support. Comparisons by LVAD indication were pre-specified exploratory analyses (destination therapy vs bridge-to-transplant). Survival analyses on LVAD support, with heart transplantation or LVAD explantation treated as censoring events, were reported. RESULTS: A total of 100 patients (mean age 58 [standard deviation 12] years, 84% male, 29% destination therapy) underwent HeartMate 3 implantation. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant aetiology (69%) and most patients (68%) were classified as INTERMACS profiles 3-4 at implantation. Over a median follow-up of 1.5 (IQR 0.5-3) years, 27 patients died on LVAD support, corresponding to a mortality incidence rate (IR) of 13.5 deaths per 100 patient-years, while 51 patients underwent heart transplantation, corresponding to an IR of transplantation of 25.4 per 100 patient-years. Five-year survival on LVAD support was 64%, with patients censored at LVAD explantation for recovery or transplantation. LVAD-related complications included bleeding (48%), infection (50%), ischaemic stroke (12%) and right ventricular failure (39%). Survival did not differ by LVAD indication (bridge-to-transplant as reference, adjusted HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.14-2.72). CONCLUSIONS: In this contemporary, real-world, medium-sized cohort, HeartMate 3 therapy provided durable long-term support across a broad spectrum of advanced heart failure patients, with outcomes consistent with those reported in large multicentre registries.

title: Corticosteroid Burden and Hearing Outcomes in Eosinophilic Otitis Media With and Without Biologic Therapy: A Pilot Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Eosinophilic otitis media (EOM) is a refractory, type 2-driven form of otitis media that often requires repeated local and/or systemic corticosteroid therapy. Biologic agents prescribed for comorbid type 2 airway disease may improve EOM outcomes; however, comparative real-world data remain limited. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate changes in EOM severity, air-conduction pure-tone average (PTA), and corticosteroid treatment burden in patients with EOM treated with and without biologic therapy in a single-center retrospective cohort. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with EOM treated at a single tertiary center. The index date was defined as initiation of biologic therapy (dupilumab or mepolizumab) in the biologics group and initiation of EOM-directed corticosteroid therapy (systemic and/or intratympanic) in the non-biologics group. Post-index outcomes were assessed within a prespecified 10-14-month window, selecting the visit closest to 12 months. The primary analysis was conducted at the patient level, averaging bilateral ear outcomes when applicable. Primary outcomes were the EOM severity score (0-10) and air-conduction PTA (0.5/1/2/4 kHz). RESULTS: Fourteen patients (24 ears) were included (mean age: 57.3±9.3 years; three men/11 women), with seven patients per group. Follow-up timing was standardized (median: 12.5 months; interquartile range [IQR]: 12.0-13.0). Baseline severity score and air-conduction PTA differed between groups (4.9±1.7 vs. 5.7±1.1; 39.6±19.0 vs. 55.0±19.0 dB, respectively). Severity improved in both groups; however, the between-group difference in change did not reach statistical significance (p=0.077). Air-conduction PTA improved within the biologics group (p=0.031); however, the between-group difference in PTA change was not significant (p=0.249). Systemic corticosteroids were discontinued in the biologics group (0.00±0.00 mg/day) but remained required in the non-biologics group (1.35±1.55 mg/day; p=0.011). CONCLUSION: In this pilot real-world cohort, biologic therapy used for comorbid type 2 airway disease was associated with a reduced corticosteroid burden and lower post-index EOM severity. Air-conduction PTA improved within the biologics group; however, the between-group difference in PTA change was not statistically significant, and the hearing findings should therefore be considered exploratory. These preliminary findings should be interpreted cautiously and may help inform adequately powered future studies.
venue: ORL; journal for oto-rhino-laryngology and its related specialties

title: Delirium in Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury and Long-Term Cognitive Decline: A Global Federated Real World Data Analysis.
abstract: Background and objective Delirium may occur in patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), but this may be a marker for subsequent cognitive decline post-TBI. We aimed to compare cognitive outcomes and all-cause mortality between TBI patients with and without delirium. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX global federated research network. We compared TBI patients who developed delirium within 14 days of TBI diagnosis with those who did not. The primary outcome was the 2-year composite risk of dementia, vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Secondary outcomes included dementia, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's disease and all-cause mortality. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed in female patients, older adults (≥ 75 years), and individuals with substance use. Results TBI patients with delirium (n = 2564; mean age, 66.6 ± 19.4 years; 59.4% male), when compared with TBI patients without delirium (n = 667,950; mean age, 48.0 ± 25.1 years; 60.3% male), had more baseline comorbidities, including psychiatric disease, cerebrovascular disease and ischemic heart disease. After propensity score matching, TBI patients with delirium, compared with those without delirium, had a higher 2-year risk of the primary composite outcome (HR, 2.47; 95% CI, 1.84-3.31), as well as dementia (HR, 2.63; 95% CI, 1.92-3.60), vascular dementia (HR, 2.76; 95% CI, 1.45-5.24) and Alzheimer's disease (HR, 2.23; 95% CI, 1.21-4.09). Conclusion Delirium following TBI is associated with an increased risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Delirium post-TBI may be a marker or a contributing factor to long-term cognitive decline in TBI patients.

title: Describing Patient Characteristics, Treatment Patterns, and Disease Burden Among Patients with Alopecia Areata in Mexico: A Secondary Analysis of the Adelphi Real World Alopecia Areata Disease Specific Programme.
abstract: Introduction Alopecia areata (AA) is a common autoimmune disease characterized by nonscarring hair loss, yet real-world data on AA in Mexico are sparse. This study aimed to characterize disease burden and identify unmet treatment needs among patients with AA in Mexico. Methods Clinical data were analyzed from Adelphi Real World's AA II Mexico Disease Specific Programme™ (October 2024-April 2025), a linked physician and patient cross-sectional survey with retrospective elements. Dermatologists provided clinical and treatment information for eight consecutive patients with AA within prespecified severity quotas (three mild, three moderate, and two severe/very severe). Patients completed the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, the Alopecia Areata Patient Priority Outcomes instrument, and the Skindex-16 AA questionnaire. Analyses were stratified by physician-assessed AA severity (mild, moderate, severe/very severe). Results Of the 319 patients included, 123 had mild, 112 moderate, and 84 severe/very severe AA. Disease duration, percent scalp hair loss, nonscalp hair loss (eyebrow, eyelash, and body), and hair regrowth at consultation differed significantly across severity groups. Traditional medications, such as intralesional, topical, and oral corticosteroids, were the most frequently prescribed treatments across all severity groups. Physician-reported satisfaction with current treatment decreased with increasing AA severity and was significantly different across severity groups (P Conclusion This study helps address the gap in real-world evidence on AA in Mexico. The reliance on traditional therapies, combined with low treatment satisfaction among physicians and patients with moderate to very severe AA, suggests a need for improved access to advanced therapies within the Mexican healthcare system.

title: Disproportionality analysis of adverse event reporting with aspirin, statins, and their co-exposure in FAERS, 2004-2025.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize and compare adverse-event reporting patterns for aspirin without statins, statins without aspirin, and aspirin-statin co-exposure in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), and to explore statistical reporting-interaction signals. METHODS: We analyzed FAERS reports from 2004 Q1 through 2025 Q1. Active-comparator disproportionality analyses compared aspirin-statin co-exposure with aspirin-without-statin and statin-without-aspirin reports using the reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and empirical Bayesian geometric mean (EBGM), followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction. Candidate preferred terms (PTs) common to both active-comparator analyses underwent adjusted statistical interaction analyses using four exposure groups, including a neither-drug reference. Primary models retained missing age, sex, and reporter type as explicit Unknown categories, and a complete-case sensitivity analysis excluded reports with missing adjustment covariates. RESULTS: After deduplication, 18,932,599 unique FAERS reports were retained. The active-comparator analysis included 134,479 aspirin-without-statin reports, 202,565 statin-without-aspirin reports, and 70,806 aspirin-statin co-exposure reports. Among 9,332 and 9,736 PTs tested in the two active-comparator analyses, 119 and 254 PTs remained after prespecified signal-detection criteria and BH-FDR correction, respectively; 42 PTs were common to both comparisons. Adjusted interaction models were reliably estimable for 40 candidates, and 31 PTs met both additive and multiplicative reporting-interaction criteria. Missingness was substantial for age (42.33%), sex (12.12%), and reporter type (4.35%). The complete-case dataset retained 53.83% of reports, and 21 of the 31 primary both-scale-positive PTs remained jointly positive. CONCLUSIONS: Aspirin-statin co-exposure showed distinct adverse-event reporting patterns in FAERS. The identified signals are exploratory statistical reporting interactions and do not establish increased incidence, clinical risk, causality, or pharmacological drug-drug interactions. Only 21 of the 31 primary both-scale-positive PTs remained jointly positive in the complete-case sensitivity analysis, reinforcing the need for cautious interpretation and validation in denominator-based pharmacoepidemiologic datasets.

title: Effect of Continuous Intraoperative Intravenous Infusion of Low-Dose Dexmedetomidine on Prognosis of Patients Undergoing Elective Neurosurgery: Study Protocol for A Single-Center, Prospective, Observational Study
abstract: Abstract Background Neurosurgical procedures are complex with high trauma and long duration, posing challenges for anesthetic management. Conventional regimens carry high complication risks. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is suitable for neurosurgical anesthesia, but the efficacy and safety of low-dose DEX (0.2 µg·kg − ¹·h − ¹) in elective neurosurgery lack large-sample prospective real-world validation, especially in non-selective populations. Methods and analysis: This single-center, prospective, non-interventional real-world study at Huzhou Central Hospital enrolls all eligible general anesthesia elective neurosurgery patients who sign informed consent, with no pre-specified sample size. It adheres strictly to routine clinical practice without modifying anesthetic protocols. Eligible patients receive low-dose DEX infusion per attending anesthesiologists' decisions. Primary outcomes are emergence quality; secondary outcomes include intraoperative hemodynamic stability and emergence-related adverse events. Linear mixed models and multivariate regression will clarify DEX's effects on perioperative prognosis and related risk factors. Discussion This trial will provide large-sample prospective real-world evidence for the standardized application of low-dose DEX in neurosurgical anesthesia. The results will help optimize perioperative management strategies, improve patient safety, and support clinical guideline updates. Trial registration: C hinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400084903. Registered on 27 June 2024.

title: Evaluating Long-Term Effectiveness and Safety of Glaucoma Surgical Innovations: A Systematic Review.
abstract: PRCIS: A systematic review examining reporting of long-term safety of glaucoma surgical innovations. 27 studies met inclusion criteria and demonstrated effectiveness over the short to medium term. Use of registries to optimise future long-term evaluation is recommended. PURPOSE: To synthesise evidence on the long-term effectiveness and safety of glaucoma surgical innovations introduced since 2004 and appraise reporting quality against IDEAL Stage 4 recommendations, designed to promote transparent study of the long-term impact of surgical innovations. METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL were searched for studies published from 1 January 2014 to 21 October 2024. Eligible studies evaluated novel glaucoma surgery with ≥2 years' follow-up and ≥100 participants. Randomised controlled trials, observational studies, registry analyses, and case series were included. Reporting was assessed using a 16-item adaptation of the IDEAL Stage 4 checklist. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and the Joanna Briggs Institute case-series checklist. RESULTS: The search strategy retrieved 1758 matches, with 27 studies meeting inclusion criteria. Procedures included iStent, Xen-45 Gel stent, Hydrus microstent, Endoscopic photocoagulation, Trabectome and Kahook dual blade. Follow-up ranged from two to six years. All studies described design and 22 reported pre-specified outcomes sufficiently; however, only four explained how missing data were handled. Intraocular-pressure and medication outcomes generally favoured the intervention, but heterogeneity in design, comparators, outcomes, and surgical context precluded pooled estimates. Adverse-event reporting was inconsistent. One cohort study was poor quality; 14 case series had unclear or unreported methodological items; and four RCTs had at least one high-risk domain. CONCLUSIONS: Glaucoma surgical innovations appear effective over the medium term, but limited long-term follow-up and inconsistent safety reporting preclude firm conclusions about comparative effectiveness and long-term safety. Standardised reporting and prospective registries are needed.

title: Explainable Machine Learning Models for Classifying Preoperative Anxiety in Patients With Femoral Neck Fractures: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: AIM: To develop and internally validate explainable machine learning models for concurrent classification of preoperative anxiety in patients with femoral neck fractures. DESIGN: Single-centre retrospective observational cohort study. METHODS: Clinical, perioperative and psychosocial data from 271 surgical admissions (270 patients) during 2024 were analysed. Preoperative anxiety was classified during the preoperative bedside assessment phase using a prespecified score greater than 8 on the anxiety subscale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Three tree-based ensemble models were compared using fivefold, patient-grouped nested cross-validation with fold-specific preprocessing, feature selection, resampling, tuning and separate probability calibration. RESULTS: Preoperative anxiety according to this prespecified definition was identified in 79 admissions. The anxiety group was older, had lower psychological resilience and perceived social support, and had greater surgical fear and frailty. The three algorithms showed similar internal discrimination, and paired comparisons did not support superiority of one model. Psychological resilience, perceived social support and surgical fear were selected in every validation fold for all models. Frailty index was selected in three of five folds for each model. CONCLUSION: The models identified a stable psychosocial feature profile for concurrent classification but require external and prospective validation before clinical use. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING PRACTICE: These findings may inform future research on structured nursing assessment of preoperative anxiety. The models should not replace validated screening or clinical judgement and require prospective evaluation before routine use. IMPACT: Psychological resilience, perceived social support and surgical fear were the most stable selected features. REPORTING METHOD: The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology and TRIPOD+AI reporting guidelines were followed. NO PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: None, because this study retrospectively analysed existing de-identified records.

title: Exploration of a simple-indicator prediction model for omalizumab efficacy in chronic inducible urticaria.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) shows variable response to omalizumab, and clinicians lack a parsimonious, clinic-friendly tool to predict benefit from routine data and early symptom change. AIM: We developed and validated a practical prediction model using easy-to-obtain indicators. MATERIAL AND METHODS: We conducted a single-centre, non-interventional cohort at The First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University, including consecutive provocation-test-confirmed CIndU patients starting omalizumab. The primary outcome was week-12 response, defined as UCT ≥ 12; non-response (UCT < 12) was the modelled event to prioritise early identification of patients unlikely to benefit. Pre-specified predictors were demographics, disease duration, subtype, baseline UCT, log2(total IgE), basic blood indices, CRP, anti-TPO, and provocation thresholds. Penalised logistic regression with multiple imputation and bootstrap validation was used. A dynamic model added week-4 change in UCT-7 (∆UCT-7). RESULTS: We analysed 557 patients; 343 (61.6%) were week-12 responders and 214 (38.4%) non-responders. The baseline model showed good performance (AUROC 0.78, Brier 0.19) and near-ideal calibration (calibration slope 0.98; intercept 0.01). Adding week-4 ∆UCT-7 improved discrimination (AUROC 0.84) and accuracy (Brier 0.16). Performance gains were consistent across major CIndU subtypes and in a temporal test set. Decision curve analysis indicated higher net benefit than treat-all or treat-none strategies at clinically relevant non-response risk thresholds. No anaphylaxis occurred and five mild adverse events were recorded. CONCLUSIONS: A simple indicator model, strengthened by an early week-4 update, provides accurate and clinically useful prediction of week-12 omalizumab response in CIndU and supports external validation and prospective impact studies.

title: Extent of Open Science Practices in the Reporting of Real World Evidence Research
abstract: Introduction: Open sharing of research methods and software code is fundamental to open science principles and reproducible research practices and has long been the norm in some scientific disciplines. Increasingly, scientific publishers are introducing policies to encourage or mandate sharing of research protocols and analytical code. Code sharing is especially important when research data cannot be shared, as is often the case in research using population data. However, the prevalence of protocol and code sharing in population data science research has been underexplored. Objectives: To assess open science practice usage by authors in real world evidence (RWE) research published in the International Journal of Population Data Science (IJPDS). Method: We reviewed RWE research articles publishing estimates of associations in the IJPDS from January 2019 to October 2024. We determined the proportion of published articles reporting (i) a link to a study protocol, (ii) a link to a pre-registered study protocol, (iii) a statement about the availability of the data, (iv) a link to the analytical code, and (iv) reference to a reporting checklist or guideline. Results: None of the 41 eligible articles met all five open science domains. One article included a link to the study protocol and none cited a pre-registered protocol. Fourteen (34%) articles included a statement about data availability. No articles included a link to the analytical code, although one included it in supplementary material and two indicated availability on request. Five (12%) articles referred to using a reporting checklist. There was no clear evidence of increasing adoption of open science practices over time. Conclusions: Researcher alignment with international best practice for open science was poor among RWE articles published in IJPDS. Potential solutions to encourage an open science culture include increasing awareness through training and education, building Communities of Practice, providing incentives and implementing open science publication policies.
venue: International Journal for Population Data Science

title: Extracting adverse event nature, severity, timelines and resulting interventions from clinical notes of patients receiving CAR-T cell therapy using large language models.
abstract: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR‑T) therapy, genetically engineered patient T cells targeting tumor antigens, has transformed care for hematologic malignancies but requires careful tracking of adverse events (AEs) often documented only in unstructured electronic health record (EHR) notes. We evaluated a Large Language Model (LLM)-based approach in UCSF's secure environment to extract AEs, dates, grades, and interventions within 30 days post‑infusion for six commercial CAR‑T products (2012-2023), benchmarking against two evaluators. Using GPT‑4‑0314 in a zero‑shot setting with four prompts (prespecified AEs, non‑prespecified AEs, CRS, ICANS), we compared outputs against dual annotations on a random sample of 50 notes using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and Cohen's kappa. From 4,762 progress notes for 293 patients (median age 65.6), CRS occurred in 80.2% (median onset 4 days); neutropenia 70.0% (16 days); neutropenic fever 64.8% (4 days); ICANS in 34.8%. Interventions included tocilizumab and corticosteroids. Grades were frequently undocumented (CRS 62.3%, ICANS 56.1%); documented cases were mainly CRS grade 1 (59.4%) and ICANS grade 2 (28.0%). Performance was high on CRS and ICANS grading (accuracy of 0.97 and 0.91, respectively). Moderate performances were assessed for prespecified AE extraction (accuracies 0.62-0.76), and non‑prespecified AEs (accuracies 0.76-0.84). Inter‑rater reliability (IRR) was strong for CRS/ICANS presence and grade (kappa 0.86-0.96), moderate for dates and interventions, and weaker for broader AE attributes. LLM‑derived insights can augment AE monitoring and real‑world evidence generation by unlocking unstructured clinical detail and characteristic timelines after CAR T. However, performance varied for broader AE attributes, warranting cautious use. Performance was highest for detecting and grading CRS and ICANS, with strong to near-perfect IRR. While cautious use of LLMs is warranted due to the variable performance observed in this study, these results support further evaluation of supervised CRS/ICANS extraction in controlled EHR-based research or pilot settings, with monitoring and prospective validation.

title: Four-Stage Data Quality Framework for Multi-Source Oncology Real-World Data Integration: Validation Using Health Datasets Mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Real-world data (RWD) quality assurance is essential for oncology research and regulatory decision-making, yet validated, multi-stage frameworks for heterogeneous, multi-source oncology RWD remain inconsistently documented. This study describes and empirically validates a regulated, four-stage data quality (DQ) framework for integrating two independent oncology real-world data sources into a HIPAA-compliant platform harmonized to the OMOP Common Data Model, supporting a pharmaceutical sponsor's Phase I proof-of-concept evaluation. Methods: A four-stage methodology—Mapping File, Structural Mapping, Conceptual Mapping, and Data Synchronization Validation—was applied across eleven OMOP CDM domains using pre-specified, rule-based SQL validation scripts under documented test protocols, aligned with GCDMP principles and the Kahn et al. DQ taxonomy. Five testing phases (Connectivity, Sanity, ETL, System Integration, Regression) were independently executed to formal sign-off criteria. Results: All five testing phases achieved a Passed outcome for both sources. Ten of eleven domains in Data Source A and all eleven in Data Source B met structural mapping criteria; four domains per source were not applicable for conceptual mapping and synchronization. The framework identified 354 patients in Data Source B with a visit record dated after death, with direct implications for survival analysis validity. Conclusion: A regulated, rule-based, four-stage DQ framework provides a reproducible, auditable mechanism for certifying multi-source oncology RWD before research or regulatory use. Detection of a clinically material temporal defect underscores the necessity of formal, pre-specified DQ assurance as a precondition for trustworthy real-world evidence generation.

title: From Adipose Tissue Dysfunction to Venous Thromboembolism.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE), driven by adipose tissue dysfunction, chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability, impaired fibrinolysis, immunothrombosis, and venous stasis. Modern incretin-based therapies induce substantial weight loss and improve multiple cardiometabolic abnormalities that may influence thrombotic risk. To critically evaluate the biological rationale and clinical evidence supporting a potential role of incretin-based therapies in modifying VTE risk, while distinguishing mechanistic plausibility from proven clinical benefit and weight-loss-mediated effects from direct pharmacological actions. Methods: Narrative review of MEDLINE/PubMed and EMBASE (2000-2026), with critical appraisal of mechanistic studies, randomized trials, pharmacoepidemiological evidence, and current clinical recommendations. Results: Experimental and translational studies provide biological plausibility for potential antithrombotic effects of incretin-based therapies through modulation of inflammation, endothelial function, platelet activation, and coagulation pathways; however, these biomarkers are not validated surrogate endpoints for VTE.
